title: A tiny GPT, deeply explained: architecture, code, training, V1-V7

slides.title: A tiny GPT, deeply explained

blocks.text: Architecture → actual Python → learning → seven version recipes → measured outcomes.
A decoder-only GPT-2-style model: 437,760–842,496 parameters, trained locally on public-domain Internet Archive OCR.

items: Main lecture: internals and experiments.
Appendix: every recorded generated sample, unedited.

slides.notes: Use the main lecture over two sessions, then browse the sample appendix during discussion. The deck is generated from source files and the three experiment JSON records. V1/V2 are scratch-trained; V3-V7 are warm-started continuations. No pretrained GPT-2 weights are used.

slides.title: What students should be able to explain

items: Trace every tensor from byte IDs to next-byte logits.
Explain causality, pre-normalization, residual paths and weight tying.
Build a training batch without future or document-boundary leakage.
Distinguish scratch training, warm starts and identity depth growth.
Read the results without confusing byte accuracy with good writing.

slides.notes: Prerequisites: Python, basic PyTorch, matrix multiplication, softmax, and gradients. Allocate a first session to architecture/code and a second to data/training/version comparisons. The appendix is searchable evidence, not material that must all be presented aloud.

slides.title: GPT-2-style does not mean pretrained GPT-2

rows: No KV cache or distributed training

blocks.text: Structurally faithful and readable; not compatible with the original GPT-2 checkpoint shapes.

slides.notes: Reference implementation: https://github.com/openai/gpt-2/blob/master/src/model.py . The reference's conv1d projections are pointwise linear maps. Our initialization and training engineering are implementation choices, not a claim to reproduce every original GPT-2 detail.

slides.title: The family at a glance

blocks.text: The core mechanism stays the same. V5 adds depth; V3–V7 mainly broaden data coverage.

slides.notes: V1 uses no dropout. All later named versions use dropout 0.1. V2 doubles context and adds a block relative to V1. V5 adds the fourth block. The vocabulary remains 256 because bytes represent new words without needing a tokenizer vocabulary update.

slides.title: Six real Archive works, not synthetic text

blocks.text: Available training data: 1,240,716 bytes, 9.4× the original corpus.

slides.notes: All scans are Internet Archive digitized books with NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT US metadata. This is not a Wayback crawl. Peter's metadata says c1911 but its title page says 1912. Rights are US-specific; Peter Pan-related material has special UK provisions. Review older language and OCR errors before classroom use. Source URLs are in the closing slide.

slides.title: Extract the story, not the whole scanned volume

items: Alice: stop before advertisements for Looking-Glass.
Peter: exclude the separately bound Margaret Ogilvy.
Keep source, cleaned and split hashes; retain uncorrected OCR errors.

slides.notes: This is actual code, not pseudocode. The verified start/end regular expressions are stored in BOUNDARIES and the corpus manifest. Missing reliable markers cause an explicit error. Decorative initial letters can be absent from OCR; the Oz opening is one example. Do not silently fill missing text with invented prose.

slides.title: Split first; never move a holdout into training

blocks.text:
def spans_for(content):
    first, second = int(len(content) * 0.8), int(len(content) * 0.9)
    spans = dict(train=(0, first), validation=(first + MAX_CONTEXT, second),
                 test=(second + MAX_CONTEXT, len(content)))
    if any(end - start <= 4 * MAX_CONTEXT for start, end in spans.values()):
        raise ValueError("Expanded book is too short for useful disjoint splits.")
    return spans
Each new work: contiguous 80/10/10 passages, with 128 discarded bytes at both boundaries.
The original train/validation/test files remain frozen.

slides.notes: A window must fit within one book's training split. The test is within-book, not an unseen-author benchmark. A 128-byte boundary gap guards the maximum context. Byte cuts need not align with words or Unicode characters; the learning task itself is defined on bytes. Checksums detect accidental changes.

slides.title: Tokenization: a deliberately visible choice

blocks.text:
def encode(text: str) -> list[int]:
    return list(text.encode("utf-8"))
“Alice” → [65, 108, 105, 99, 101]. A Unicode character can occupy several bytes.
256 IDs, no unknown-word token. Byte perplexity is not GPT-2 BPE perplexity.

slides.notes: decode uses replacement characters for invalid or unfinished UTF-8. Generation can terminate mid-character or mid-word. Keeping bytes makes the Transformer visible without a tokenizer subsystem, but makes context much shorter in word terms. For cross-tokenizer comparisons, use normalized raw-byte metrics rather than token PPL.

slides.title: A training example is a shifted window

blocks.text: x = A l i c     y = l i c e. Every training position predicts the next byte.
The sampled start leaves room for the final target: len(data) − context.

slides.notes: starts are sampled from [0, len(data)-context), so y's largest possible index is len(data)-1. This is why the input and target share a window shifted by one. The helper receives only a training document, never a concatenation crossing validation or a book boundary.

slides.title: The full computation graph

blocks.text: V7: B=32, T=128, C=128, H=4, L=4. The loss trains all positions.
Generation uses only the final position’s logits, then appends one sampled byte.

slides.notes: Residual connections preserve the [batch, time, channel] shape throughout the stack. Token and position embeddings are added, not concatenated. Logits are unnormalized scores; cross-entropy combines log-softmax with the correct-target lookup.

slides.title: Tensor shapes inside one attention block

blocks.text: Scores alone contain 2,097,152 floats ≈ 8 MiB per block, before gradients.

slides.notes: Head width is C/H=32. Time appears twice in the score tensor: one axis for query positions and one for keys. Doubling context multiplies score memory by four, not two. Total training memory also includes activations, gradients and optimizer states.

slides.title: Learned embeddings and positions

blocks.text: Embeddings: token table [256,C], position table [context,C]. Positions start at zero.
Layer blocks preserve width; positional information is learned, not sinusoidal.

slides.notes: Inspect GPT.__init__ for the two nn.Embedding tables. These are absolute learned positions like GPT-2. During cropped generation, positions reset for each window; this is a simplification, not a long-context or cached-decoding implementation.

slides.title: Project Q, K and V; split the heads

blocks.text: One linear layer makes 3C features; chunk separates query, key and value roles.

slides.notes: Q identifies what each position seeks, K describes positions to match against, and V provides their content. view splits C into heads and head-width; transpose puts heads before time. Each head gets an independent attention matrix, not independent tokens.

slides.title: The triangular mask is the causality guarantee

blocks.text: 1 = visible key; 0 = forbidden future key. A token may see itself and all earlier tokens.
Changing positions 8–15 must leave logits at positions 0–7 unchanged.

slides.notes: Rows are queries and columns are keys. Mask the future before softmax with minus infinity, so forbidden weights become zero. Zeroing scores instead would still give future keys probability mass. Evaluation disables dropout for the exact-prefix test.

slides.title: Scale, mask, normalize, then mix values

blocks.text:
scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(width // self.heads)
scores = scores.masked_fill(~self.mask[:length, :length], float("-inf"))
weights = self.attention_dropout(scores.softmax(dim=-1))
softmax(QKᵀ / √head_width) V. Scaling prevents large dot products from saturating softmax.

slides.notes: The scale is 1/sqrt(32) for our 128-wide, four-head models. Before dropout, each attention row sums to one over visible keys. Training-time attention dropout scales surviving weights and does not renormalize the row. This is separate from the causal mask.

slides.title: Merge heads and project back to the residual width

blocks.text:
attended = (weights @ v).transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(batch, length, width)
return self.output_dropout(self.project(attended))

self.heads = config.heads
self.qkv = nn.Linear(config.width, 3 * config.width)
self.project = nn.Linear(config.width, config.width)
self.attention_dropout = nn.Dropout(config.dropout)
self.output_dropout = nn.Dropout(config.dropout)
transpose → contiguous → view merges head outputs. The projection restores the C-wide residual interface.

slides.notes: After transposing the attended values, contiguous makes the memory layout compatible with view. The output projection mixes heads. Its output dropout is a regularization site, not a change in tensor shape or vocabulary.

slides.title: A block has two pre-normalized residual branches

blocks.text:
self.mlp = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(config.width, 4 * config.width),
    nn.GELU(approximate="tanh"),
    nn.Linear(4 * config.width, config.width),
    nn.Dropout(config.dropout),
)
Attention communicates across time. The MLP transforms each position’s features.

slides.notes: Pre-LN means normalize the branch input, then add its output to the untouched residual stream. LayerNorm normalizes features within one token, not across time. The MLP is position-wise: C→4C→C, with tanh-approximate GELU between its linear maps.

slides.title: Why LayerNorm and GELU are not optional details

items: LayerNorm(x) = gain·(x−μ)/√(variance+ε) + bias; statistics are across C.
GELU approximately gates x by the probability it exceeds a Gaussian threshold.
The residual path carries existing information and a direct gradient route.
Final LayerNorm precedes the tied vocabulary projection.

blocks.text: Our nn.LayerNorm default ε is 10⁻⁵; GELU uses approximate='tanh'.

slides.notes: Contrast LayerNorm with BatchNorm: its behavior does not depend on another example in the minibatch. GELU is not ReLU; it retains a smooth negative-side response. These operations are preserved from the GPT-2 structural pattern.

slides.title: One embedding matrix serves two jobs

blocks.text:
# F.linear uses the very same matrix as the input token embedding.
logits = F.linear(x, self.token.weight)
loss = None
if targets is not None:
    loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, 256), targets.reshape(-1))
return logits, loss
F.linear(x, token.weight) uses the same [256,C] parameter matrix used for input lookup.

slides.notes: Weight tying reduces parameters and connects token representations with token prediction. F.linear interprets the embedding matrix as output rows. The loss flattens [B,T,256] and [B,T] so every target contributes. No softmax is needed before F.cross_entropy; supplying probabilities there would be incorrect.

slides.title: Count the parameters instead of guessing
slides.notes: Attention contributes 4C²+4C parameters; the MLP contributes 8C²+5C; two LayerNorms contribute 4C. The final norm adds 2C. Dropout and the causal mask have no learned parameters. There is no second output vocabulary matrix.

slides.title: Initialization keeps residual branches controlled

blocks.text:
for block in self.blocks:
    nn.init.normal_(block.attention.project.weight,
                    std=0.02 / math.sqrt(2 * config.layers))
    nn.init.normal_(block.mlp[2].weight,
                    std=0.02 / math.sqrt(2 * config.layers))
Linear/embedding weights start with σ=0.02; residual projections use σ=0.02/√(2L).

slides.notes: Biases are zero. Scaling residual output projections with depth controls accumulated residual variance. This is our training-oriented implementation choice, not a promise to match the original TensorFlow checkpoint initialization exactly.

slides.title: Where V2–V7 apply dropout

blocks.text: model.eval() disables dropout, but does not disable gradients. no_grad() is a separate control.

slides.notes: V1 has p=0, so its legacy function is unchanged. The same saved state dict loads with a default dropout field when old checkpoints omit that field. The dropout tests check train/eval behavior, generation determinism and training-mode restoration.

slides.title: One optimization step

blocks.text:
optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
_, loss = model(x.to(device), y.to(device))
if not torch.isfinite(loss).item():
    raise RuntimeError(f"Nonfinite {spec['name']} loss at step {step}")
loss.backward()
norm = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
if not torch.isfinite(norm).item():
    raise RuntimeError(f"Nonfinite {spec['name']} gradient at step {step}")
optimizer.step()
AdamW LR=0.0003 for new stages; weight decay=0.01; clip gradient norm to 1.

slides.notes: The scratch studies used LR=0.001. Expanded stages use a lower fixed LR because they warm-start learned weights. zero_grad precedes backward; clipping follows backward and precedes optimizer.step. Nonfinite loss or gradients raise an explicit error.

slides.title: Score next bytes without giving away the target

blocks.text:
for indices in positions.split(64):
        offsets = torch.arange(-model.config.context, 0)
        x = data[indices[:, None] + offsets].to(device)
        y = data[indices].to(device)
        logits = model(x)[0][:, -1]
        losses.extend(F.cross_entropy(logits, y, reduction="none").cpu().tolist())
        correct += int((logits.argmax(-1) == y).sum().item())
finally:
    model.train(previous_mode)
Inputs end immediately before the scored target. Only logits[:,−1] is compared with that target.

slides.notes: Evaluation positions are sampled without replacement using fixed generators. All versions score identical targets within a comparison but may use different context lengths. Conditioning on prior held-out bytes is normal autoregressive evaluation, not training on test targets. eval and no_grad serve different purposes.

slides.title: Add one work per version

blocks.text: The original training file is rehearsed; its validation/test bytes are never added to training.

slides.notes: V3 adds Alice; V4 Oz; V5 Peter; V6 Willows; V7 Secret Garden. Each stage trains on the cumulative allowed training documents. All per-document splits are frozen before training. These volumes are unique available training bytes, not repeated exposures.

slides.title: Checkpoint lineage is not optimizer lineage

blocks.text: Load parent weights → create a fresh AdamW optimizer → train → select by common validation.
V1 is independent. V3–V7 inherit selected weights, not parent optimizer moments.

slides.notes: All stages use seed 42, but they are not independent seeds or scratch runs. The parent SHA-256 is saved for each version. Executed updates can exceed the selected checkpoint's update count; inherited learning is based on the selected state.

slides.title: Warm starts plus controlled depth growth

blocks.text:
def grow_depth(parent, layers):
    if layers < parent.config.layers:
        raise ValueError("Depth growth cannot remove existing blocks.")
    model = GPT(replace(parent.config, layers=layers)).to(parent.token.weight.device)
    state = model.state_dict()
    state.update(parent.state_dict())
    model.load_state_dict(state)
    # New residual branches start as identity, preserving the parent's inference.
    for block in model.blocks[parent.config.layers:]:
        nn.init.zeros_(block.attention.project.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(block.mlp[2].weight)
    return model

slides.notes: This is the entire helper. It only permits adding blocks. Existing state tensors are copied, then new attention and MLP output projection weights are zeroed. Their biases already initialize to zero. With dropout disabled, the new residual branches add zero, preserving the parent's inference function before training.

slides.title: A new block starts as identity, but can learn

blocks.text:
def test_depth_growth_preserves_function_and_new_branch_can_learn(self):
    parent = GPT(Config(context=16, width=32, layers=2, dropout=0.1)).eval()
    x = torch.randint(256, (2, 16))
    expected = parent(x)[0].detach()
    grown = grow_depth(parent, 3).eval()
    torch.testing.assert_close(grown(x)[0], expected, rtol=0, atol=0)
    self.assertEqual(grown.config, replace(parent.config, layers=3))
    grown(x, torch.randint(256, (2, 16)))[1].backward()
    self.assertGreater(grown.blocks[2].attention.project.weight.grad.abs().sum().item(), 0)
    self.assertGreater(grown.blocks[2].mlp[2].weight.grad.abs().sum().item(), 0)
    torch.testing.assert_close(parent(x)[0], expected, rtol=0, atol=0)
    with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
Zero output weights do not freeze the branch: output projections receive gradients on the first step.

slides.notes: Upstream parameters in a zero-output branch initially get no gradient through that zero projection; after the projection begins learning, their gradients can flow. The test checks exact inference preservation and nonzero gradients on both output projection matrices. Parent parameters are not aliased or modified.

slides.title: Choose a document before choosing its window

blocks.text: P(original)=0.5; P(each new book)=0.5 / number_of_new_books.

slides.notes: Rehearsal deliberately oversamples the small original document. It aims to reduce forgetting of the original style while sharing the rest of the windows across new works equally, not proportionally to their byte lengths.

slides.title: No batch row crosses a book boundary

blocks.text:
for index in chosen.unique().tolist():
    rows = (chosen == index).nonzero().flatten()
    x[rows], y[rows] = batch(documents[index], context, len(rows), rng, "cpu")
return x, y, chosen
Group selected rows by document; call the original shifted-window helper for that document only.

slides.notes: x and y are assembled after document-local sampling. Concatenating documents and sampling arbitrary windows would create artificial transitions and could cross holdout boundaries. The tests use constant-valued synthetic books to make any crossing immediately visible.

slides.title: How much each document is actually sampled

blocks.text: Random mixture counts are recorded, rather than assumed to equal their expected percentages.

slides.notes: Every row is a 128-byte context with 128 shifted targets. Windows are sampled with replacement and overlap within the training partition. Available training bytes and total presented bytes are different quantities.

slides.title: The same weighted score selects every new version

blocks.text: loss = 0.5·original_loss + 0.1·(Alice + Oz + Peter + Willows + Garden losses).

slides.notes: combine averages losses and accuracies with explicit weights, then computes PPL=exp(averaged loss), not average(per-book PPL). The five-book macro prevents the longest book from dominating. The original gets half the selection weight by design; it is not an unbiased corpus-size-weighted benchmark.

slides.title: Aggregate gains do not mean every domain improved

items: V6 improves Willows, but Alice, Oz and Peter accuracy each fall slightly from V5.
V7 improves Garden, while Willows falls from V6.
A rehearsal mixture protects the original book; it also biases the learning objective.
Data, depth and cumulative compute are bundled: no causal attribution from this study.

slides.notes: The actual per-book tables make these reversals visible. V6→V7 Willows goes from about 56.7% to 56.2%, despite improved macro accuracy. A model with broader training is not automatically superior for every target distribution.

slides.title: Training loss is not a generalization guarantee
slides.notes: Train diagnostics use fixed sampled training targets with dropout disabled, not the noisy last minibatch loss. The first and expanded studies use different diagnostic sample sizes, so treat train gaps as qualitative evidence, not a controlled gap benchmark. A small context and repeated book exposure still permit overfitting.

slides.title: Generate by repeatedly predicting the last position

blocks.text:
for _ in range(count):
        logits, _ = self(tokens[:, -self.config.context:])
        logits = logits[:, -1].float() / temperature
        cutoff = logits.topk(top_k).values[:, -1:]
        logits = logits.masked_fill(logits < cutoff, float("-inf"))
        # CPU sampling gives a reproducible RNG on CPU and Apple MPS.
        next_token = torch.multinomial(logits.softmax(-1).cpu(), 1, generator=rng)
        tokens = torch.cat((tokens, next_token.to(tokens.device)), dim=1)
finally:
    self.train(training)
Crop to context; recompute learned positions; sample; append; repeat.

slides.notes: The model is set to eval; generation uses no_grad and a local CPU sampling generator. After generation it restores the previous train/eval mode. No KV cache is used, so the full cropped window is recomputed for every emitted byte.

slides.title: Temperature and top-k do not change learned quality

items: Temperature τ scales logits: probabilities = softmax(logits / τ).
Lower τ sharpens probabilities; higher τ adds randomness.
Top-k suppresses all but the k highest-scoring byte logits.
Every recorded sample uses τ=0.8, k=40, 240 generated bytes, fixed seeds.

blocks.text: Reported loss/accuracy use raw model logits, not temperature or top-k filtering.

slides.notes: Decoding can make samples look cleaner while leaving held-out predictive scores unchanged. Fixed seeds make a controlled qualitative comparison; they do not make one sample representative of all outputs. Invalid UTF-8 can be produced.

slides.notes: These are unedited outputs for the same prompt, seed and decoding settings. Both can contain recognizable clauses while failing grammar or story continuity. A 100% training-lexicon hit rate can coexist with nonsense. The appendix contains every recorded output so the visible examples are not the only evidence.

slides.title: What the 16 tests and artifact checks establish

items: Future bytes do not change earlier logits; shifted targets stay in the split.
Loss/backpropagation work; a toy sequence can be learned.
Old checkpoints still load; dropout/generation modes are restored.
Document windows cannot cross books; exact-span overlap and checksum changes are detected.
Added depth preserves inference initially and has learnable output branches.

slides.notes: Test sources: test_model.py and test_expanded.py. report_expanded.py reloaded all seven models, reproduced all 35 expanded samples and both metric suites, and checked parent lineage plus frozen artifacts. These checks establish implementation correctness and reproducibility, not general intelligence.

slides.title: What the evidence does and does not support

items: Supports: learned local language and better held-out next-byte prediction.
Does not support: a reliable chatbot, factual answers or coherent long stories.
Limits: one seed, short contexts, within-book holdouts, OCR noise, repeated validation.
Next: clean/diverse books, byte-level BPE with comparable BPB, multi-seed ablations, fresh document-level tests.

slides.notes: The strided 128-byte audit found no matches in 2,406 checked holdout spans but is not exhaustive semantic deduplication. The original test was published repeatedly. Do not tune further on the fresh expanded test and continue calling it fresh. Future RoPE/cache/fused-attention lessons should distinguish quality from efficiency.
